newsitem.title: USA: US, EU meat talks go down to wire, but prospects dim.
newsitem.headline: US, EU meat talks go down to wire, but prospects dim.

text.p: Talks between the United States and the European Union to settle a trans-Altantic dispute over meat and poultry inspection methods appeared on Thursday to be spilling over into the Easter holiday weekend.
But U.S. officials said it would take almost a miracle for negotiators to reach an agreement in the so-called verterinary equivalency talks by a rapidly approaching April 1 deadline.

"Right now, there is a high degree of pessimism based on the apparent lack of flexibility demonstrated by the Europeans," said a senior Agriculture Department official, who did not want to be identified.
"It's looking like it's going to take something pretty extraordinary to get any agreement by April 1," said Joel Brandenberger of the National Turkey Federation.

Negotiators have been meeting in Washington all week to resolve the years-old dispute which could threaten several hundreds of millions of dollars worth of trade in meat, poultry, dairy, eggs and pet food.

At the core of the issue is how Washington and Brussels deal with the different U.S. and EU meat and poultry safety inspection methods. An agreement would allow each side to accept products from the other even if their inspection methods differ.

Agriculture Department officials held separate briefings with the meat, poultry and dairy sectors throughout the day to put together a package of counter proposals to send back to EU negotiators Thursday night. Another meeting between the two sides was scheduled for Friday.
What will happen on April 1 if an agreement has not been reached is still unclear, but most observers expect trans-Atlantic meat and poultry trade to be disrupted to some degree.
U.S. industry officials and several farm-state lawmakers are urging the administration to take tough action against Europe if the issue is not settled.

"We have absolutely no choice here ... We have been more than reasonable for over a decade," said Nick Giordano of the National Pork Producers Council. The pork group is calling for a cutoff of U.S. imports of European pork if there is no agreement.
The EU has said it would implement new veterinary and sanitary controls for imports on April 1, and the United States has said it would retaliate for any loss of access to EU markets.

Some $50 million worth of U.S. poultry shipments to the EU could be curtailed if the EU adopts new standards, and Washington could potentially halt the imports of over $200 million worth of European pork.
Some $350 million worth of U.S. pet food exports to Europe could also be affected, but industry officials said most of the issues pertaining to pet food appear to have been resolved.
